q1226: Long stress keeps the body's stress system running for months, and over time the normal daily cortisol rhythm can become disturbed or even flattened. Sleep becomes less refreshing, blood sugar can swing, and the brain feels foggy. Burnout includes exhaustion, cynicism and a sense of being ineffective. Pushing harder with caffeine and willpower tends to lead to crashes. ME/CFS is different, a real biological illness in which symptoms get worse after effort, so graded push-through exercise is not recommended. Other medical causes such as anaemia, thyroid problems or sleep apnoea also need checking by a doctor. For both burnout and ME/CFS, pacing helps, breaking tasks into small chunks with rest before tiredness peaks. Over weeks, this steadier rhythm lets the nervous system and energy systems slowly recover.
q1227: God designed our bodies with limits, and those limits are not flaws. They are part of what makes us creatures who depend on Him. Fatigue signals that we have been running beyond our design, sometimes because of overwork and sometimes because of illness we did not choose. God's answer is not shame but rest. Sabbath was His idea, given as a gift, not a burden. This reflects His character. He is patient, gentle with the weak and never in a hurry. The slow work of pacing mirrors the way He restores us, little by little. Learning to rest before you crash, and to receive help, teaches deep trust. In that trust, our worth is found in being loved, not in what we produce, and wholeness grows.
q1228: God describes His own love in the language of caring for a baby. "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee" (Isaiah 49:15). "As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you" (Isaiah 66:13). The psalmist pictures a soul "quieted... as a child that is weaned of his mother" (Psalm 131:2), and Jesus "took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them" (Mark 10:16). Responding warmly to a crying baby is not spoiling. It is reflecting the heart of God. A baby's earliest experience of being held and answered becomes their first picture of a God who hears and comforts.
q1229: A baby's brain grows astonishingly fast in the first year, forming vast numbers of new connections. The brainstem and emotional brain lead the way, while the thinking brain has barely begun. Babies cannot calm themselves yet, so they borrow calm from their caregivers through a process called co-regulation. When a parent responds to crying, rocks, sings and holds, the baby's stress hormones tend to settle and their nervous system learns what safety feels like. "Serve and return" moments, smiling, talking and copying their sounds, build pathways for language and connection. Predictable rhythms help the body clock develop. Over months, these repeated experiences shape a secure attachment, which research links with better emotional regulation, relationships and learning later in life. Your own calm is part of their care.
q1230: God designed babies to be completely dependent, and that is not a weakness in His plan. It is the very way love is learned. Through countless small moments of being fed, held and soothed, a child discovers that the world is safe and that they are wanted. This design reflects God's relational heart. He did not create us to grow alone but within loving bonds, just as He exists in the eternal love of Father, Son and Spirit. Parents, too, are being shaped, learning patience and selfless love. Because a baby borrows calm from you, caring for yourself and accepting help is part of the design. These early months lay foundations of trust that can point a child, for life, toward the faithful love of God.
q1231: Scripture shows that God is patient with immaturity. "Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him. For he knoweth our frame. He remembereth that we are dust" (Psalm 103:13-14). God knows what we can and cannot yet do, and parents are called to share that understanding. Paul writes, "Fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4). James urges every believer to be "slow to speak, slow to wrath" (James 1:19). Staying calm and close during a tantrum, naming feelings and offering simple choices reflects this patient, nurturing love. God meets our own outbursts with steady kindness, and parents can offer the same to their little ones.
q1232: In toddlers, the emotional brain is racing ahead while the thinking brain that manages impulses and plans is years from mature. This means toddlers feel enormous feelings with very little ability to stop them. When a tantrum strikes, the emotional brain floods and reasoning goes offline, so long explanations do not help in the moment. A calm parent nearby acts as an external brake, and through co-regulation the child's stress system gradually settles. Naming feelings, such as "You're so cross the tower fell," links emotion to words and, over time, helps build pathways for self-control. Simple choices and predictable routines reduce stress and power struggles. Thousands of these repeated experiences, across the toddler years, slowly strengthen the child's own ability to calm down.
q1233: God designed children to grow gradually, and the toddler years show this clearly. A small child discovering that they are a separate person, saying "no" and exploring everything, is part of healthy development, not rebellion. God made the brain to develop from the bottom up, with feelings first and self-control later, so that children would need loving adults for many years. This design binds families together and teaches parents patience, humility and grace. It reflects God's own patience with us as His children, as He teaches us slowly and lovingly over a lifetime. When parents respond to big feelings with calm rather than shame, they model the gentle strength of God and help their child grow toward emotional wholeness.
q1234: Jesus welcomed little children with warmth. "Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 19:14). God told parents to talk about His words "when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up" (Deuteronomy 6:7). Proverbs 22:6 says, "Train up a child in the way he should go." And for fears, David prays, "What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee" (Psalm 56:3). Reading Bible stories, praying simply, taking fears seriously and never using God as a threat all reflect this welcoming heart. Children this age are forming their first lasting pictures of God, and He wants those pictures to be full of love.
q1235: Between three and five, language and imagination develop rapidly. Children begin to name feelings and follow simple rules, but self-control is still fragile, especially when they are tired or hungry. Because fantasy and reality are still mixed, fears of monsters or the dark feel very real to their brains. Play is how young children learn. Through it they practise language, problem-solving, sharing and managing emotions, strengthening many developing brain networks. Simple "when-then" phrases give clear structure without long lectures, which they cannot yet process. Teaching calm-down tools like slow breathing helps them practise regulating their nervous system. Specific praise for effort encourages persistence. Over months, these consistent experiences help build self-control, confidence and a secure sense of being loved.
q1236: God designed young children to be full of wonder, questions and imagination. Their constant "why?" reflects a mind made to seek truth and meaning, and ultimately to seek Him. Their fears, though sometimes inconvenient, give parents the opportunity to show them how to find comfort and trust. God made children to learn through play and relationship rather than through instruction alone, because He is a relational God who teaches through love and example. A parent kneeling to help a frightened child or playing on the floor together reflects God's humility in coming close to us. When limits are clear and kind, children learn that love and boundaries go together. This becomes a foundation for knowing God as both loving and good.
q1237: Scripture shows that growing in skill and belonging is part of God's plan. Of Jesus Himself we read, "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man" (Luke 2:52). Paul warns, "Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged" (Colossians 3:21), and encourages believers to "comfort yourselves together, and edify one another" (1 Thessalonians 5:11). Children at this stage are deciding whether they are capable and whether they belong. Giving real responsibilities, praising effort and character, and praying together about real worries reflects God's pattern of entrusting His people with small tasks and growing them through faithfulness. He meets children through parents who make love unconditional and gently strengthen them for life.
q1238: During the school years, the thinking brain matures significantly, allowing children to plan, reason and understand fairness. Friendships and school success matter more, and children begin to judge themselves. Research suggests that the way parents speak to children often becomes the voice they use toward themselves. Praise for effort rather than fixed ability tends to help children keep trying after setbacks. Giving responsibilities and allowing natural consequences, within safe limits, builds the brain's problem-solving networks and a sense of competence. Asking specific questions about their day keeps connection strong. Snacks and play before homework help the tired brain recharge. Over months and years, these patterns shape a resilient sense of self and the skills to handle challenges.
q1239: God designed children to grow into capable people who contribute, and the school years are a key season for that. He made them with a strong sense of fairness, which reflects the justice of God's own character. Their desire to belong reflects that they were made for community. When parents let children try, struggle and sometimes fail, they mirror God's way of growing us. He does not do everything for us, but walks beside us as we learn. When love is not tied to grades or performance, children experience something of God's grace, the truth that they are loved before they achieve anything. This frees them to work hard without fear, and it builds a healthy, whole identity rooted in being loved.
q1240: Scripture honours young people and the changes they go through. Paul told the young Timothy, "Let no man despise thy youth, but be thou an example of the believers" (1 Timothy 4:12). At twelve, Jesus stayed behind in the temple asking questions, and His parents, though worried, listened and He grew in wisdom (Luke 2:41-52). The boy Samuel learned to hear God's voice with Eli's gentle help (1 Samuel 3). The psalmist says, "I will praise thee, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psalm 139:14). Explaining puberty honestly, affirming who they are and keeping the door to faith open all reflect this respect. God meets preteens through steady adults who stay close without pushing, as their bodies and minds change rapidly.
q1241: Puberty brings surges of hormones that change the body and the brain. The emotional and reward centres become more sensitive, so moods swing and peer approval suddenly feels enormous. Meanwhile, the thinking brain that weighs consequences is still developing. This mismatch helps explain self-consciousness, intense reactions and new interest in privacy. Research suggests that warm, stable connection with parents protects preteens through these changes. Talking side by side in the car or while walking can feel less intense than face-to-face conversations, making it easier to open up. Accurate information before changes happen reduces fear and shame. Clear, explained rules give structure without heavy control. Over these years, steady support helps the developing brain build healthy patterns of emotional regulation and decision-making.
q1242: God designed the body to change before the brain fully catches up, and this gives children a season of needing guidance even as they gain independence. It is a bridge between childhood and adulthood. This design reflects God's wisdom in growth. He does not rush us into maturity but walks us through gradual change. The preteen's desire for privacy and their own views is part of forming a personal identity and faith, which God values because He wants a real relationship, not mere rule-following. When parents stay steady, respectful and loving through eye-rolling and moods, they model God's unshaken love. This helps preteens accept their changing bodies as good gifts and grow toward whole, secure adulthood.
q1243: Scripture gives a beautiful picture of parenting older children in the prodigal son story. While his son "was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). The father allowed freedom, yet his home remained a safe place to return. Ecclesiastes 12:1 urges, "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth," and the psalmist says, "thou art my trust from my youth" (Psalm 71:5). Proverbs 22:6 encourages training a child in the way he should go. Coaching rather than controlling, sharing your faith honestly and repairing quickly after conflict reflect this pattern. God meets teenagers with patience, giving them roots of love and wings of growing freedom.
